summary: Adds a codecs parameter to media types that can contain different formats, so the content type alone tells a receiver which codecs are needed to play it. Receivers can then decide whether to accept the content, transcode it, or fetch a codec. It is a standards-track document that was later replaced by RFC 6381.

eli5.summary: A video file can be like a box with a mystery inside. This adds a label telling which kind of player is needed, so you know before opening it.

questions: how to specify codecs in mime type
what is the codecs parameter in mime types
what is a bucket media type
subtitle: A codecs parameter that lets a media type label say which codecs are inside a container before anyone opens it.

tldr.problem: Types such as video/3gpp can hold many different audio and video formats, so a receiver must inspect the content to know whether it can play it.
tldr.mechanism: A new optional codecs parameter on the Content-Type lists every codec used, as dot-separated elements, with a name space defined for ISO Base Media File Format files.
tldr.outcome: Servers and constrained devices can decide to accept, transcode or fetch codecs from the label alone. This document was later obsoleted by RFC 6381.

today: RFC 4281 was a Proposed Standard published in December 2005 and has been obsoleted by RFC 6381, which is now the place to look for the codecs parameter.

sections.title: The Problem with Bucket Types
sections.content:
Some media types are bucket types: the type and subtype only say it is a container, not which formats are inside. The RFC gives examples. video/3gpp may hold H.263 Profile 0, H.263 Profile 3, H.264 or MPEG-4 Simple Profile video, and AMR, AMR-WB, Extended AMR-WB, AAC or Enhanced aacPlus audio. A video/3gpp file might not even contain video.

Checking each media element to learn the codecs is slow. It burdens Multimedia Messaging (MMS) servers that must decide whether content needs transcoding, and it burdens devices with limited memory, processing power or bandwidth, such as cellular telephones and PDAs.
sections.eli5: Imagine every lunchbox looks the same from outside. You would have to open each one to find out if it holds something you can eat.

sections.title: The Codecs Parameter
sections.content:
The codecs parameter is added to audio/3gpp, audio/3gpp2, video/3gpp and video/3gpp2. It is optional in all of them, and future ambiguous types are strongly encouraged to include it. The value is a single codec identifier or a comma-separated list. Each identifier has dot-separated elements: the MIME type fixes the name space of the first element, and each element fixes the name space of the next.

The parameter MUST contain all codecs indicated by the content and MUST NOT list codecs not used by any media element. Receivers may still need special handling, since not every listed codec is always essential (alternative language tracks or droppable timed text, for example). The parameter must be complete in breadth, but systems MUST NOT rely on it being complete in depth, because a code's hierarchical rules may have been written after a server was implemented.

If the parameter lists codecs that are not present, a receiver SHOULD discard it. If it misses codecs, the receiver MAY discard it.
sections.eli5: The label lists every kind of player needed, no more and no less. If the label looks wrong, you can ignore it and check the box yourself.

sections.title: Syntax and Encoding
sections.content:
There are two forms. The simple form, codecs=value, is used when no octets need encoding. The second form, codecs*, uses the MIME parameter encoding of RFC 2231: the value usually starts with two single quotes (no character set or language), and each octet needing encoding is written as a percent sign plus two hexadecimal digits. A list with commas must be enclosed in quotes, and implementations MUST NOT add whitespace between tokens except after a comma. The period is reserved as the hierarchy delimiter.

The RFC gives these generic examples: codecs=a.bb.ccc.d and codecs="a.bb.ccc.d, e.fff".
sections.eli5: Normally you just write the names with dots between the parts. If a name has a strange character, there is a special way to write it safely.

sections.title: The ISO File Format Name Space
sections.content:
This RFC only defines values for the ISO Base Media File Format family. The first element is a sample description entry four-character code registered with the MP4 Registration Authority, and values are case sensitive.

If the first element is mp4a (MPEG-4 audio) or mp4v (MPEG-4 part-2 video), the second element is the hexadecimal ObjectTypeIndication, with the leading 0x omitted. For mp4a with value 40 the third element is the audio object type in decimal, so AAC low complexity, value 2, is mp4a.40.2. For mp4v with value 20 the third element is the video ProfileLevelIndication in decimal, so MPEG-4 Visual Simple Profile Level 0, value 9, is mp4v.20.9.

Other media types can adopt the parameter by updating their registration, and a new document may define additional name spaces.
sections.eli5: The name is like a code on a sticker: the first part says the family, and the next numbers say exactly which model.

sections.title: Examples and Security
sections.content:
The RFC shows complete headers such as Content-Type: video/3gpp; codecs="s263, samr" (H.263 video plus AMR audio) and Content-Type: audio/3gpp2; codecs=mp4a.E1 (13k audio). For extra details like pixel counts or color depth, it points to the Content-Features header.

The parameter does not alter the security considerations of the media types it is used with. An incorrect value could cause content to reach a device that cannot render it, or to be withheld from one that can, so it can enable some denial-of-service attacks. The RFC notes this most likely happens by accident, since an attacker who can alter media in transit could do more harm by changing the media itself.
sections.eli5: A wrong label could send you the wrong lunchbox, but it is usually just a mistake and not a trick.

data.title: Codecs parameter examples
data.code:
Content-Type: video/3gpp2; codecs="sevc, s263"
Content-Type: audio/3gpp; codecs=samr
Content-Type: video/3gpp; codecs="s263, samr"
Content-Type: audio/3gpp2; codecs=mp4a.E1
Content-Type: video/3gpp2; codecs="mp4v.20.9, mp4a.E1"
